title: SOC 2 & BCDR tabletop + KMS/residency review - Delta Insurers
summary: Redwood ran a tabletop focused on SOC 2 surface area and BCDR with Delta Insurers. Key concerns were KMS/BYOK, audit log retention and privileged access, plus concrete RTO/RPO targets and escalation routing. Agreed action items include a focused runbook draft, a security architecture diagram that shows key custody, and an engineered failover test plan.

transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-08-14
- Time: 16:00 UTC
- Duration: ~62 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan Blake (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Aisha Patel (CISO, Delta Insurers), Tom Ramos (Head of Platform), Lena Ortiz (SRE), Marcus Lee (Compliance)

Summary (auto): SOC 2 scope + BCDR tabletop; discussed KMS BYOK, audit log retention, RTO/RPO targets, SLA credits, and escalation routing.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on. I'm Jordan Blake from Redwood, AE on the account. With me is Maya Chen, our solutions engineer.
[00:18] Maya: Hi all. Quick agenda — SOC 2 scope hygiene, on-prem / VPC KMS patterns, then we'll run a short tabletop around a region outage and talk through RTO/RPO and escalation.
[00:32] Aisha: Sounds good. From Delta's side we've got a couple of priorities: KMS/BYOK control, long term audit retention for 7 years, and a clear SLA mapping to our contracts team.
[00:45] Tom: Also want to make sure the failover doesn't blow up our downstream billing reconciliation jobs; those are sensitive to partial replays.
[00:56] Jordan: Absolutely. Maya, can you kick off with how Redwood handles key custody and HSM integration?
[01:05] Maya: Yep. At a high level Redwood supports both Redwood-managed KMS and customer-managed BYOK via external KMS — we integrate with cloud KMS like AWS KMS, Google CMEK, and HSMs via the KMS API. We can also integrate to an H S M or external key manager if you have one on-prem. Note — some of the enrollment flows require us to exchange a public key and do a wrap/unwrap flow.
[01:32] Marcus: When you say wrap/unwrap flow, is Redwood ever in a position to decrypt customer data? Like are keys in our control?
[01:40] Maya: For BYOK the customer retains the master key. Redwood will hold ephemeral session keys and encrypted blobs. In practice we never store plaintext model context or the customer master key. If you choose Redwood-managed keys, then Redwood will hold the KMS material — that's common for hosted customers but for regulatory workloads we recommend BYOK with HSM.
[02:02] Aisha: For Delta we're mandated to have the master keys under our control, ideally an HSM with split custody. We also need an attestation of who can request key rotations and procedure.
[02:14] Jordan: We can provide a runbook for key rotation and the RBAC controls required to trigger rotation. It plugs into SSO + SCIM for role-based privileges.
[02:24] Tom: Speaking of RBAC, what's the current support for SAML + SCIM provisioning and fine-grained roles for audit log access?
[02:32] Maya: We support SAML SSO for authentication and SCIM for provisioning. Roles are mapped to service scopes — admin, operator, auditor, read-only. Audit log access is governed by the RBAC layer and we can limit visibility to the log service to auditors only. Note there is a separate retention policy setting for logs.
[02:54] Lena: What's your default retention? We need 7 years immutable.
[03:00] Maya: Default is 90 days in the platform, with options to export to a customer log archive (S3) or send to your SIEM. For long term retention we recommend log export to your archival bucket with object lock for immutability. We also support streaming to Splunk/Elastic.
[03:19] Marcus: Do you provide proof of deletion / chain-of-custody? Our legal team will ask.
[03:25] Jordan: We have audit entries for deletion actions, and for BYOK we can produce key rotation/change logs. We can also produce a custody manifest on request as part of the compliance package.
[03:40] Tom: Okay, shifting to BCDR — what RTO/RPO numbers are realistic for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private?
[03:50] Maya: Good question. Rough numbers we've seen: Hosted mode (multi-region fallback) targets RTO around 1-2 hours for session rehydration depending on KV cache behavior, RPO is near-zero for stateful store if you replicate; but for very large prefix caches you can accept degraded performance. For Dedicated reserved pools you can get RTO ~30-45 minutes if you have warm standby, RPO depends on your replication frequency — often under 15 minutes. For Private on-prem it's highly variable — typical guidance is plan for RTO 2-6 hours and RPO 4+ hours unless you implement synchronous replication.
[04:31] Aisha: Our contractual RTO requirement is 1 hour for critical services, RPO max 15 minutes. That seems to push towards Dedicated with warm standby.
[04:42] Maya: That aligns — Dedicated with a cross-region DR standby and automated routing policies should hit those targets. We should map the specific data plane components: model binaries (redeployable), KV cache (rebuildable), and persistent logs/metrics (replicated).
[04:58] Jordan: Let's do a quick tabletop. Scenario: a zonal outage in primary region takes down a Dedicated pool. Walk through detection, failover, and who we call. Maya, start.
[05:10] Maya: Detection — health checks trip, telemetry shows increased latency and queue buildup. Automated policy routes traffic to standby region after X consecutive failures. If policy can't route (e.g., capacity), we fall back to a cheaper model variant or queue requests with a degraded SLA.
[05:31] Lena: Who owns the escalation? PagerDuty or Redwood first? Our ops want to know where to page.
[05:36] Jordan: Our standard is two-tier; Redwood has SRE on-call via PagerDuty for platform faults and also a dedicated account engineer for P1s during business hours. For enterprise contracts we can bind escalation to your primary on-call via a joint runbook.
[05:51] Tom: We need to make sure billing and reconciliation jobs are paused or replayed safely. Does Redwood provide a safe replay mechanism?
[05:59] Maya: We don't replay customer transactions; we provide idempotency tokens and at-most-once delivery semantics at the ingress layer. For downstream batch jobs, we can coordinate a drain window and provide an event watermark so you can resume.
[06:15] Marcus: On SLA credits, can you summarize the credit formula? Our procurement will push back if it's vague.
[06:21] Jordan: SLA is tiered. For Dedicated enterprise, typical is 99.95% with credits scaling by duration of downtime; we can surface the exact schedule in the contract addendum. For hosted customers it's 99.9%. We'll share the SLO vs credit matrix post-call.
[06:38] Aisha: Ok. Next, audit log access — in an incident, who gets pushed logs? Do we have tamper-evident trails?
[06:47] Maya: Logs are append-only with checksums in the storage backend; exports carry a manifest and signing option. We also maintain an audit trail with actor, TID, timestamp and IP for each action which can be zipped for e-discovery.
[07:04] Lena: Forensics — how quickly can Redwood pull raw logs for a P1?
[07:09] Maya: We can extract and deliver within 2-4 hours for critical incidents; if you've set up direct SIEM streaming it's near-real-time.
[07:19] Tom: What about data residency? We're obligated to keep EU customer data in EU regions.
[07:25] Jordan: Redwood supports region pinning and VPC private deployments. For EU residency you'd select an EU region and Redwood can restrict model and logging storage to that region; for full isolation we recommend Private deployment inside your VPC.
[07:40] Marcus: Are there restrictions on model variants in Private? We need some models not allowed in EU due to licensing.
[07:47] Maya: We support model whitelisting per deployment; you can pin versions and restrict model catalogs. For licensing restrictions we can provide a deployment manifest.
[07:58] Aisha: Back to BCDR — what tests do you run in production to validate failover?
[08:04] Maya: We offer canary failovers and synthetic traffic tests. For Dedicated enterprise customers we can run scheduled DR rehearsals where we trigger the failover in a controlled window, measure RTO/RPO and validate health checks. We recommend quarterly tabletop + annual full rehearsal.
[08:24] Lena: If we do an annual full rehearsal, is there support for rollback if downstream systems fail?
[08:29] Jordan: Yes, runbooks include rollback and cutover decision gates: automated health checks + manual approval points. We'll coordinate with your SREs for rollback criteria.
[08:41] Marcus: For compliance evidence, what documentation will Redwood produce after a rehearsal?
[08:46] Maya: We provide a rehearsal report: timestamps of trigger/route, metrics for RTO/RPO, any manual interventions, logs extracted, and a post-mortem template.
[08:58] Tom: Sounds good. A couple of curveballs — legal asked about subpoena/third-party requests. If Redwood gets a lawful request, how is Delta notified?
[09:07] Jordan: We notify customers per our data access and subpoena policy; for enterprise we can run notification windows and provide a point-of-contact for escalations. We also will push for narrowing requests and notify if any production access is required.
[09:20] Aisha: We'll need that policy text. Also service continuity during partial credential compromise — what are the worst-case steps?
[09:28] Maya: If credentials are compromised, we recommend immediate rotation of impacted keys, revoke sessions, and a targeted failover to a standby region. For SCIM/SAML compromises we can revoke OIDC tokens and force a re-provision. We keep a session affinity TTL short to limit sessions.
[09:45] Lena: Forcing rotation at scale is painful. Do you have automation to rotate and re-encrypt caches without full downtime?
[09:52] Maya: Yes — key rotation flows allow re-wrapping of session keys while keeping the wrapped blobs in place; worst case you rebuild KV caches progressively so it's rolling rather than do a big-bang outage.
[10:07] Tom: Let's nail contact points — who do we page for P1, P2, P3?
[10:12] Jordan: P1: Redwood SRE on-call + AE escalation; P2: Redwood platform eng + account ops; P3: standard ticket queue. We'll map severity definitions to your SRE definitions in the runbook.
[10:24] Marcus: We'll want a signed agreement for contact SLAs in the contract appendix.
[10:28] Jordan: Understood — we'll mark that as deliverable.
[10:33] Maya: Quick note on metrics — for the rehearsal report we'll capture: time to detect, time to route, time to green (successful health check), error rate during failover, and token loss if any.
[10:47] Aisha: Good. Also, our compliance team wants to confirm that Redwood's SOC 2 scope includes the model serving layer and the control plane.
[10:56] Jordan: Yes — Redwood's SOC 2 covers control plane, infra used for hosted inference, and operational controls — we'll share the SOC 2 summary and an inventory mapping to the system components. That will be in the package.
[11:08] Tom: One last question — is there a maximum time that private on-prem deployments can be out of sync before data loss risk increases?
[11:16] Maya: That depends on replication mode; async replication increases RPO. We recommend synchronous or near-sync for any state required for strict RPOs; otherwise plan for data drift and compensating reconciliation jobs.
[11:29] Jordan: Okay we'll summarize and assign owners. Action items noted. Any final comments?
[11:35] Aisha: Please include the BYOK enrollment steps in the doc you send. Also we'd like a short checklist for auditors describing where to find logs and export manifests.
[11:45] Jordan: We'll include a BYOK checklist and an auditor checklist.
[11:49] Tom: Thanks everyone.
[11:51] Jordan: Thanks all, we'll follow up with docs and schedule the follow-up tabletop.

End of transcript.
